# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Traditional View of Toughness

College students described toughness as hard-nosed, gritty, playing through pain, stoic, showing no signs of distress, persevering. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance came out on top. The typical image is a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back into place, or Craig MacTavish (last NHL player to play without a helmet, retired 1997), or a wounded military hero. Traditional toughness means overcoming obstacles with perseverance, discipline, and stoicism—often pictured as a strong brute of a man.

## Bobby Knight’s Model

Bobby Knight won over 900 games (third most all-time), reached five Final Fours, won three NCAA championships. His 1976 Indiana team went undefeated. Knight defined toughness as “Being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” His teams pioneered a pressing man-to-man defense. But his methods included: tampons hanging from lockers of players he thought “soft”; frequent cussing; a 1991 tirade (“This is absolute fucking bullshit… I’ll fucking run your ass right into the ground”); bringing toilet paper with shit to show players what he thought of them; choking a player at practice. His definition of toughness was founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing through obstacles, using fear to establish authority and control.

## Authoritarian Parenting

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1960s) classified parenting styles by two factors: responsiveness (attuned, supportive, acquiescent to children’s needs) and demandingness (maturity demands, supervision, discipline). Permissive parents are low demandingness, high responsiveness. Authoritarian parents are high demandingness, low responsiveness—relying on fear, threats, punishment, one-way communication (“do this because I said so”). In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally.” 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft on their children. The “just right” Goldilocks fit is high demand accompanied by warmth and understanding. We’ve taken the demanding part and forgotten warmth, care, and responsiveness.

## Callousness and Machismo

Toughness language: “soft,” “hardening up,” “show no signs of weakness.” In youth sports, parents justify making eleven-year-olds go until they puke as “necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior” (Mark Hyman, *Until It Hurts*). Toughness is tied to masculinity: “man up,” “stop being a pussy,” “There’s no crying in baseball!” (A League of Their Own). The image is The Rock or Vin Diesel—brute strength, confidence, bravado. But women, who research shows handle pain better than men, may have had the correct definition all along.

## Consequences of Callous Toughness

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair (19) showed signs of profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches yelled “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” It took 34 minutes to get him off the field, another 28 to call 911. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke. Rhabdomyolysis (damaged muscle products leaking into bloodstream) has become common from extreme workouts designed not to improve fitness but to “test” athletes. Professor B. David Ridpath: the true notion is “to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots.”

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, higher substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport, it’s linked to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, fear of failure. In a study of 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse than peers from nurturing environments. The style creates the appearance of discipline without fostering it. One young athlete: “Coaches use exercise as punishment… I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished”—motivation to avoid punishment, not internal desire.

## Redefining Toughness

The old model trains us to respond to fear and power. Remove fear and control, and the “tough” individual lacks skills to navigate adversity. Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance. Real toughness is “experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.”

Pete Carroll (one of three coaches to win both NCAA championship and Super Bowl) believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, bouncing back. He uses “always compete” practices but teaches skills to handle adversity: “Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do.” Other successful coaches with humanistic styles: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D’Antoni (“We keep it positive here”). Ken Reed: “For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight… I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach.”

2008 research on nearly 200 basketball players found that “the ‘keys’ to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie… with the coach’s ability to produce an environment which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service.” Real toughness is teaching, providing a tool set to handle adversity. It means working with body and mind, facing reality, using feedback, accepting emotions, developing flexible responses. Navigating discomfort—sometimes going through, around, under, or waiting.

## The Author’s Personal Story

The author describes a race (Don Bowden Mile) where he collapsed with paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—vocal cords shut on inhalation instead of opening. Diagnosed by Dr. Stephen Miles after dozens of tests. The American Thoracic Society cites “strong emotions” and stress as triggers. The author’s previous strategy of pushing until he puked backfired. He had to learn to relax and keep breathing, neck, and mind steady at the moment of highest discomfort. This search for what toughness really means became the book.

## Four Pillars of Real Toughness

1. Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality
2. Listen to Your Body
3. Respond Instead of React
4. Transcend Discomfort

Real toughness isn’t about performing better or dealing with pain alone—it’s about becoming a healthier, happier human being. It’s attainable to all, not reserved for the talented. As podcaster Rich Roll: “Everybody goes through shit in their life. Nobody escapes obstacles.”

# Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

## Basic Categories

Seven primary types of things to track: Projects list, project support material, calendar actions and information, Next Actions lists, Waiting For list, reference material, Someday/Maybe list.

**Hard edges are critical.** Each category represents a discrete type of agreement with yourself. If categories blend—e.g., reference mixed with to-read items, or calendar items mixed with next actions—you go psychologically numb to the contents. The categories must be kept visually, physically, and psychologically separate.

**All you really need are lists and folders.** Lists track projects, someday/maybes, and actions. Folders hold reference and project support. Don't impose external priority scaffolding that requires constant rearrangement—prioritize intuitively against shifting variables. A "list" can be: (1) a file folder with separate notes, (2) a titled paper in a loose-leaf organizer, or (3) an inventory in software.

## Organizing Action Reminders

### Calendar Actions
Calendar shows only the "hard landscape"—time-specific ("10:00–11:00 meet with Jim") and day-specific ("Call Rachel Tuesday"). Resist putting actions on the calendar that you'd like to do but might not; the calendar must be sacred territory. Most actions belong in "as soon as possible" categories.

### As-Soon-As-Possible Actions by Context
Organize by the tool, location, or situation required. How discrete categories need to be depends on (1) how many actions you track and (2) how often you change contexts. With 25 next actions, one list might suffice; with 50–100, you need sorting.

**Common categories:**
- **Calls** – all phone calls; record phone numbers alongside each item.
- **At Computer** – actions requiring a computer. Allen maintains a separate Online list for when he flies without Wi-Fi.
- **Errands** – e.g., "Get stock certificates from bank deposit box," "Pick up suit at the tailor," "Buy flowers for Robyn." Sublists within items (e.g., "hardware store" with appended items) are useful. Location-based reminders exist but are overoptimistic for total trust.
- **At Office** – actions requiring physical presence (e.g., purging a filing cabinet). With "hotel-ing" on the rise, you may need At Office A and B lists.
- **At Home** – e.g., "Hang new watercolor print," "Organize travel accessories," "Switch closets to winter clothes." If you work only at home, At Home suffices.
- **Agendas** – for people and meetings. Keep separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children, attorneys, financial advisers, etc. Standing meetings (staff, board, committee) deserve their own lists. Add ad hoc as needed.
- **Read/Review** – longer-than-two-minute reading items. Best managed in a physical tray or portable folder. Some professionals also use a Review/Respond category. For digital input, a Review/Watch file or Surf Web action list can hold links.

### Waiting For
Track deliverables others are responsible for (e.g., tickets ordered, scanner coming, OK on proposal). Include the date requested and any agreed-upon due date—"But I placed the order March twentieth" is worth its weight in gold. Keep this list close to Next Actions lists; responsibility may bounce back and forth.

### Using Original Items as Action Reminders
Some inputs serve as their own reminders. Paper examples: Read/Review tray for magazines, "Bills to Pay" folder, "Receipts to Process" envelope. For e-mail: create @ACTION and @WAITING FOR folders that sort to the top of your navigator bar. Getting e-mail "in" to empty means deleting, filing, doing <2-minute responses, and moving actionable e-mails to @ACTION. **Caution:** distributing triggers across folders, lists, and e-mail is OK only if you review all categories equally. Digital data offscreen can disappear as a prompt, causing some to revert to paper for trust.

## Organizing Project Reminders

### The Projects List
A comprehensive index of open loops—every commitment requiring more than one action step. Not for plans or priority sorting; you can't do a project, only its action steps. Real value lies in complete weekly review.

**Value:**
- Critical for control and focus—"I've got to get my driver's license renewed" can take as much mental space as "I need to formulate the agenda for next year's conference."
- Alleviates subtle tensions from projects that morph unexpectedly (e.g., registration problems, invoice disputes).
- Core of the Weekly Review.
- Facilitates relationship management—triggers constructive conversations about resource allocation.

**Where to find hidden projects:**
1. **Current activities** – calendar meetings, action lists, workspaces. Example: a conference call about a client request → "Look into possible custom program for Client XYZ." Also proposals, forms, broken watches.
2. **Higher-horizon interests** – professional accountabilities, goals, strategic plans, personal life (kids, retirement, partner's aspirations).
3. **Current problems, issues, opportunities** – problems (always projects), process improvements, creative/capacity-building opportunities. Examples: "Look into improving Frederick's relationship with his school," "Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance," "Get closure on compensation dispute with business partner."

**Subsorting options:** Personal/Professional (but personal needs weekday review), Delegated Projects (for senior managers), Specific Types (e.g., "Projects—Presentations" for speakers, sales relationships in progress). How you group matters less than completeness and regular review.

**Subprojects:** If big pieces are dependent (e.g., "Upgrade the kitchen" waits on "Assess electrical system"), keep the major project on the Projects list and subpieces in support material. If independent (e.g., "Finalize the patio"), you may list them separately. Allen's example: "Move to Amsterdam" was one project for months, then unpacked into fifteen as things became immediate.

### Project Support Materials
Resources to support actions and thinking—not reminders. Don't use support material for reminding; that creates subliminal chant: "Do something about me!" First add the project to Projects list, put actions on appropriate lists, then pull support when doing the action. For the Weekly Review, pull the file and check for missing next actions. Client folders and CRM software often mix reference with actions—actions belong on action lists.

**Organizing ad hoc project thinking:** Attached notes in software, e-mail folders (e.g., "Johnson Partnership—Active" and "Johnson Partnership—Archive"), paper-based files, loose-leaf notebook pages. The danger of digital options is spreading data into too many places without coordinating links. Clear out stale notes.

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

### Reference Materials
Once you distinguish actionable from nonactionable, reference is just your library—no psychological weight. Systems include general-reference filing (1–4 physical drawers, dozens of e-mail folders), large-category filing (e.g., a whole drawer for gardening), contact managers (purely reference—don't use for action reminders), and libraries/archives at personalized levels. Allen keeps restaurant lists in software with hundreds of folders. The only issue is whether material is worth the time and space to keep.

### Someday/Maybes
Track things to reassess later—e.g., "Learn Spanish," "Get Marcie a horse," "Climb Mt. Washington," "Write a mystery novel," "Get a vacation cottage." Populate from creative imagination and current projects. Subcategorize if useful (e.g., home projects vs. bucket-list fantasies). Avoid "Hold and Review" files—people hold but don't review.

**Using the calendar for future options:**
- Triggers for activating projects (e.g., product launches, annual conferences, birthdays).
- Events you might want to participate in (seminars, social events).
- Decision catalysts for major decisions (hire/fire, merge/acquire, change job/career, strategy redirection). "It's OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system."

**Tickler file:** 43 folders (31 daily + 12 monthly). Daily files in front starting with tomorrow's date; monthly files behind. Each day, empty the daily folder into your in-tray and refile it at the back. Allows you to "mail" physical reminders to yourself on future dates. Requires one-second-per-day behavior.

## Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders

Checklists serve as "recipes of potential ingredients" for projects, processes, events, and areas of responsibility. "Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them" (Alfred North Whitehead). Atul Gawande's *The Checklist Manifesto* is referenced.

For fuzzy commitments like "Exercise more regularly" or "Maintain good morale on my team," first identify inherent projects and actions. Then blueprint key areas of work and accountability—career goals, family, health, finances, creative expression, etc. The more novel the situation, the more control required. Checklists can be temporary (e.g., when taking on unfamiliar responsibilities like accounting, computers, marketing, legal, administration). Be open to creating checklists for anything: job areas, travel, weekly review, training programs, key clients, people to stay in touch with, year-end activities, personal development, even jokes.
